thread.title: Fitbit CEO: The Versa Watch Is Helping ‘the Entire Product Line’

author: David Marino-Nachison
title: Fitbit CEO: The Versa Watch Is Helping ‘the Entire Product Line’
text:
Photo: Fitbit By David Marino-Nachison Aug. 1, 2018 4:54 p.m. ET The Fitbit (FIT) the company hopes to become looks pretty different from the company it is today. But investors seem cool with the current version—at least, for the moment, with the shares up about 3% in after-hours trading following the release of Q2 financial results that beat Wall Street’s expectations.
The Barron’s Next 50 company said quarterly revenue came in at $299 million with non-GAAP net losses finishing at $0.22 per share. Wall Street was looking for a loss of $0.24, with the company having guided investors to the $0.23-$0.27 range.
Sales were seen coming in at $285 million, according to FactSet, the midpoint of management’s $275-$295 million guidance. Higher average selling prices, driven by a shift toward smartwatches instead of trackers, were the main factor in the revenue upside, CFO Ron Kisling told Barron’s Next.
Newsletter Sign-up “I’m really proud of the company's performance,” CEO James Park said in an interview with Barron’s Next. “We’re continuing to execute on our transition plan and deliver on our commitments to investors.”
The second half is generally more important to Fitbit, and the company now believes it could turn a profit in the next six months. Management today gaveQ3 guidance more upbeat than the Street’s latest forecast, with the company eyeing a slim net profit and revenue that could come in as high as $390 million. (FactSet’s latest estimate was $378 million.)
Fitbit has seen the boom in smartwatch popularity—in large part due to the Apple (AAPL) Watch—accelerate its own move into the category. Smartwatches accounted for 55% of revenue in Q2, and Fitbit had previously thought they wouldn’t top 50% before the second half.
But what the company hopes is that other sources of revenue, namely recurring subscription dollars from consumers or partnership revenue from health care or other organizations, will come to represent a meaningful chunk of its business.
For now, that doesn’t amount to much business: Fitbit has said non-device revenue would be “relatively immaterial” in 2018. It’s currently working to boost Versa smartwatch production to avoid the sellout it saw in Q2. (It said in June that it sold 1 million Versas since launch, but Kisling declined to update that number today.)
“When we launched Versa, we looked at our best forecasts and took ind of a conservative view,” Kisling said. “It sort of exceeded our expectations. With that increased demand, we’re adding additional production capacity .…We believe that will better match our supply with the demand that we now see.”
More About Barron’s Next Learn more about Barron’s Next The Barron’s Next 50 Fitbit shares had risen in 2018 after the company reported Q1 results that also beat expectations. That, along with the warm reception to the Versa, helped the shares to a 2018 rise of some 25% as of early June.
But they gave up those gains amid concerns about profitability, competitive pressure on the device front, and the departure of its previous CFO; they were down a few points as of the market’s close, trailing the S&P 500 .
Park said Fitbit believes the brand is increasingly attractive to consumers. “The success of Versa is providing benefits across the entire product line, he said. “From our vantage point, it’s just important that people are buying Fitbit in general.”
Corrections & Amplifications
Fitbit’s CFO is Ron Kisling. An earlier version of this post mistakenly said it is William Zerella.
